summary: Defines Sensor Measurement Lists, a simple data model for reporting sensor measurements and device parameters. It has representations in JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI. A record can carry things like a name, unit, value and time, so small devices and the systems reading them can exchange readings in a common form.

plainLanguage.summary: SenML gives sensors and the systems that collect their readings a shared data format. Its records can include a name, unit, value, and time, with shared base fields to avoid repeating information.

subtitle: A shared, compact data model for sensor readings and device parameters.

tldr.problem: Small devices need to send measurements efficiently, while receiving systems need a consistent way to interpret readings from many devices.
tldr.mechanism: SenML represents data as an array of records with short labels for names, units, values, and times. Base fields apply to following records, and the same model has JSON, CBOR, XML, and EXI forms.
tldr.outcome: The format can also carry configuration and actuation requests, but it provides no security by itself. RFC 8428 has been updated by RFC 9100.

today: RFC 8428 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9100. Its data model has JSON, CBOR, XML, and EXI representations.

sections.title: What SenML Is For
sections.content:
Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) is a data model and set of media types for simple sensor measurements and device parameters. It is designed for small processors and efficient collection of readings over protocols such as HTTP or CoAP.

A SenML Pack is an array of Records. A Record can identify a sensor, state a measurement and unit, and give the time. The format is intended for simple measurements, not every complex measurement model.
sections.plainLanguage: SenML gives sensors and collection systems a common way to describe simple readings. A record can identify what was measured, the unit, the value, and when it was measured.

sections.title: Compact Messages and Batches
sections.content:
SenML aims to carry simple measurements from many constrained devices in small messages. The RFC describes a goal of implementation in roughly 1 KB of flash on an 8-bit microprocessor.

A Pack can batch measurements from one or more sensors or from one sensor at different times. A Base Name can be written once and prepended to later record names, reducing repeated data in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Small devices can group readings into one message and avoid repeating a sensor name in every record. This reduces message size while keeping the data self-describing.

sections.title: Records and Their Fields
sections.content:
SenML has base fields and regular fields. A base field applies to its record and later records until another record supplies that same base field. A regular field applies only to the record where it appears.

The base fields include Base Name, Base Time, Base Unit, Base Value, Base Sum, and Base Version. Regular fields include Name, Unit, Value, Sum, Time, and Update Time. A value can be numeric, Boolean, text, or binary data. Each record normally has exactly one value field unless it has a Sum field.
sections.plainLanguage: Base fields provide shared information for several records; regular fields describe one record. This lets a Pack state a common name or unit once and apply it to later readings.

sections.title: Time, Values, and Cumulative Sums
sections.content:
A record's Time is added to Base Time, and its Value is added to Base Value. Missing parts of these pairs count as zero. A time below 268,435,456 is relative to now; a time at or above that value is an absolute time relative to the Unix epoch.

The Sum field represents an integrated total over time in the measurement unit multiplied by seconds. SenML can also describe configuration or actuation: a target may interpret records as requests to set named resources to values at specified times.
sections.plainLanguage: A time can be relative to when a reading is sent or based on the Unix epoch. A Pack can also carry a cumulative measurement or, when a target supports it, a request to change a device setting.

sections.title: Four Ways to Encode the Same Model
sections.content:
SenML defines JSON, CBOR, XML, and EXI representations. JSON uses short text labels such as n for Name and v for Value. CBOR uses integer labels for compactness; XML represents fields as attributes, and EXI encodes the XML structure in binary form.

The representations carry the same SenML model, but their sizes differ. In one RFC example containing multiple records, the listed sizes are JSON 573, XML 649, CBOR 254, and EXI 161 before compression.
sections.plainLanguage: SenML has readable text, compact binary, and XML-based encodings. Each expresses the same fields, though the encoded message sizes can differ.

sections.title: Extensions, Streams, and Fragments
sections.content:
Implementations MUST ignore unknown fields unless a label ends with an underscore, in which case they MUST report an error. All records in a Pack use the same version, and a reader MUST NOT use a version it does not understand.

SenSML is an optional streaming form that lets a receiver process a record as soon as it arrives. A fragment identifier can select record positions, but each selected record still needs the earlier base fields that apply to it.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can process SenSML records as they arrive, without waiting for the full stream. A selected record still depends on any earlier base fields that apply to it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SenML does not protect the data it carries. The surrounding protocol must provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication when the data or its use requires them. This matters especially when a Pack can change a system or affect the physical world.

Stable unique names can make devices or their data easier to correlate. The RFC advises using such identifiers with care or avoiding them when appropriate. Keeping a Pack intact also matters when records rely on base fields.
sections.plainLanguage: SenML does not encrypt or authenticate a message. Use security from the carrying protocol when readings are sensitive or records can control a device, and consider whether stable names reveal too much.
